title: Two Number Ones
one_liner: Two stakeholders have just asked, in the same hour, for their work to be the team's top priority next sprint. Both have reasonable cases.
brief:
## The setup

Thursday afternoon. You're refining the backlog for next sprint's planning on Monday. Two separate Slack messages, twenty minutes apart.

First: Yetunde Mbeki (COO) — 'We need the audit-trail enhancement in the next sprint. The external auditors arrive on the 14th and we need it shipped before then. This is the highest priority.'

Second: Folake Adeyemi (Head of CX) — 'Bumping the customer-portal SSO migration up to top priority for next sprint please. Three of our top-12 customers have asked about it this week and we're losing renewal conversations.'

The sprint can hold one major story plus a handful of small ones. Both audit-trail and SSO migration are major. Both stakeholders are senior. Both think they've made their case.

The team's actual capacity is the audit-trail OR the SSO migration plus small work. Not both. The previous PO would have run a WSJF on it and shown the numbers; that's an option for you too, but Yetunde finds frameworks unsatisfying and Folake has used WSJF herself to justify exactly the opposite call.

You have about three hours before you need a backlog ready for refinement tomorrow morning.

## Your turn

First move?
objective: Make the call. Land it with both stakeholders in a way that the loser understands why and the winner doesn't gloat. Have one specific thing to offer the loser that isn't 'next sprint'.
curveball: Both stakeholders are right in their own frame. The actual deciding factor is something neither has surfaced: the audit-trail work has a hard external deadline (the 14th, ten working days from now), while the SSO work has a soft renewal-conversation deadline (you can renegotiate; auditors you cannot). If the user goes to Yetunde and Folake separately to surface this — 'help me understand if the audit deadline is movable' / 'help me understand which renewals are at immediate risk if SSO slips two sprints' — the answer becomes clear: audit-trail wins this sprint, SSO becomes top of next sprint with a written commitment to Folake. If the user picks without that discovery, they may pick correctly but the loser will not feel heard.

personas.name: Yetunde Mbeki
personas.position: Auditors are in on the 14th. The audit-trail is the priority
personas.fear: Being unprepared for an external audit because the product team didn't deliver

personas.name: Folake Adeyemi
personas.position: Three top-12 customers are asking about SSO; renewal conversations are happening now
personas.fear: Losing customer renewals because the product team prioritised internal work over customer-facing work

green: Talked to Yetunde and Folake separately BEFORE making the call — pulled the hard-vs-soft-deadline information neither had volunteered
Made the call (audit-trail this sprint) and explained the reasoning to Folake first, with a specific commitment for next sprint
Did not use a framework as the justification — used the deadline reality as the justification
Closed the loop with both stakeholders in writing, with the trade-off named explicitly
yellow: Ran a WSJF score and presented the framework output as the answer — works mathematically; doesn't address the relationship
Did both, partially — split the team across both stories and missed the audit deadline by two days
Picked by escalating to your manager rather than making the call yourself
Made the call privately and let Yetunde and Folake find out at refinement Friday morning
red: Capitulated to whoever messaged second (the recency effect)
Promised both as top priority and then quietly de-scoped during the sprint
Asked the team to vote on which to do — pushes a PO decision onto the team
Sent Yetunde and Folake into a meeting with each other to 'work it out between them'
